originality.rationale: Compared claims and implications across archival excitable-media theory, the published all-graph matched-coloring period-divisibility theorem, the exact Heawood dual-channel period table, and Petersen/Frucht finite comparisons. Divisibility does not supply existence, counts, sharp minimum or uniqueness; the Heawood table is for n=14; the other graphs do not establish the specified minimum over connected cubic bipartite graphs. An accessible history of the twelve-vertex connected cubic bipartite classes concerns a different update rule. Exact graph6 string and relevant period-pair searches identified no covering record. The first-claimed minimal coexistence conclusion thus survives the available overlap checks, with explicit historical-priority risk. A final direct graph6 and paired-numerical semantic-index search returned no covering statement; this is not treated as proof of uniqueness.
residual_risks: An unindexed prior enumeration of the exact same twelve-vertex graph and both CCA/GHM eventual periods could exist; bibliographic absence is not a uniqueness proof.
Original 1993 archival preprint full text could not be materially inspected, although the accessible abstract describes lattice phase diagrams rather than this exact graph census.
Petersen result was inspected as indexed metadata, not its entire published manuscript; it concerns a nonbipartite graph and a different one-channel statement.
No independent external mathematical audit has been performed.

value.rationale: In the established matched-coloring comparison of excitable graph models, general period divisibility and a known n=14 Heawood two-channel example motivate asking when two genuinely different halving ratios first coexist in a natural regular bipartite network. The result gives both a sharp minimum graph order and uniqueness up to isomorphism, plus exact labeled-state populations for each channel. It separates the one-channel behaviors at smaller and alternative equal orders, an intrinsic minimal example and complete finite classification rather than an arbitrary individual numeric parameter. The statement is valuable without claiming a universal high-order characterization.
